editor.title: Benedictus Richard Ricardo, on the record.
editor.lede: I work where operations are complex, ownership is distributed, and the cost of confusion is real. The role is usually some mix of investigator, systems builder, and execution stabilizer.
body: Good systems do not feel complicated when they are used. They make the next step obvious, reduce wasted motion, and let people act with more confidence under pressure.
I am studying Data Science at Universitas Terbuka and continuing to refine the way process design, evidence, and execution fit together.

automation-mandate.documentTitle: The Automation Mandate · The Operational Record
automation-mandate.metaDescription: Built reporting and SOP systems that removed 12+ hours of weekly manual work at Home Digital Indonesia.
automation-mandate.title: The Automation Mandate
automation-mandate.deck: Built reporting and SOP systems that removed twelve-plus hours of weekly manual work — turning a person-dependent reporting cycle into a shared, repeatable rhythm.
automation-mandate.imageAlt: Operational dashboards showing weekly reporting metrics — the evidence the rebuilt cycle measured against.
automation-mandate.caption: Operational dashboards used to illustrate the weekly reporting cycle. Photograph used as illustration.
automation-mandate.lead: A cross-functional reporting cycle was spending too much time on repeated manual work. The fix was a structured reporting pipeline supported by clearer operating rules.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: Finance, sales, and operations were handling recurring reporting work through manual collection, repeat formatting, and fragile handoffs. The process worked — but it consumed too much time and depended too heavily on individual memory. Each week the same cycle started again, often from scratch, with the same near-misses.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: I treated the workflow like an operational system, not just a spreadsheet. The recurring workbook logic was rebuilt in Excel, the supporting SOPs were standardized so the same routine ran every cycle, and the reporting path was mapped end-to-end. The point was not the workbook; the point was that the team could run it the same way every Monday without thinking about it.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: The team removed roughly twelve hours of manual work from the weekly rhythm. The bigger shift was confidence: a cleaner cadence, fewer avoidable delays, and a process that could be maintained across functions instead of rediscovered each cycle.

automation-mandate.pull: The team removed roughly twelve hours of manual work from the weekly rhythm — and replaced it with a routine.
evidence: Built automated reporting systems in Excel that removed roughly 12 hours of weekly manual work.
Standardized SOPs across finance, sales, and operations to reduce friction during recurring reporting cycles.
Shifted the work from person-dependent repetition toward a shared operating routine.

impact.label: Hours saved weekly
impact.note: Manual reporting effort removed from the recurring cycle.

impact.label: Functions aligned
impact.note: Finance, sales, and operations on one structure.

impact.label: Shared routine
impact.note: Automation and SOPs combined into a repeatable weekly flow.

kpi-governance-record.metaDescription: Led 34 members across 10 divisions through a KPI rhythm at SMA Santa Maria 2.
kpi-governance-record.title: A council of thirty-four learns to keep time.
kpi-governance-record.deck: How a student presidency adopted a KPI rhythm — and started running like an institution instead of a friendship group.
kpi-governance-record.imageAlt: A speaker addresses a small audience in a workspace setting — used to illustrate institutional leadership and program design.
kpi-governance-record.caption: Leadership in a working setting — used as an illustration for institutional rhythm and program design.
kpi-governance-record.lead: A 34-member council across 10 divisions needed stronger rhythm, accountability, and program structure. A KPI-based governance approach gave leadership and execution a cleaner cadence.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: Once a student organization becomes multi-division, informal leadership stops being enough. The council needed clearer visibility, more consistent follow-through, and a way to evaluate programs as they went — not only after the fact.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: A more explicit governance model with measurable expectations, recurring checkpoints, and alignment between division work and institutional objectives. The council moved to a KPI rhythm with weekly reviews, clearer division expectations, and a stronger institutional planning approach for school-wide programs.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: A council that could finally see what was moving, what was blocked, and where leadership energy needed to be applied. Programs ran with more stability — including outreach that engaged twelve feeder schools — because the operating cadence held under load.

kpi-governance-record.pull: It is easier to lead a team when the team can see what it is doing.
evidence: Led 34 members across 10 divisions through a structured KPI-based governance rhythm.
Designed long-term institutional programs that were adopted at the school level.
Directed outreach and campaign activity that engaged 12 feeder schools.

impact.label: Members led
impact.note: Leadership scope across the full organization.

impact.label: Feeder schools reached
impact.note: Scale of one major outward-facing campaign.

large-scale-event-ops.documentTitle: Large-Scale Event Ops · The Operational Record
large-scale-event-ops.metaDescription: Live execution stable across 1,000+ attendee environments; MC-led Youth Mass 2025 for 500+ participants.
large-scale-event-ops.title: When the room is watching, the only thing visible is what fails.
large-scale-event-ops.deck: Three years of stage and backstage work for audiences of one thousand and more — and a Youth Mass for five hundred, MC-led.
large-scale-event-ops.bylineRole: Stage Coordinator & MC · Ultimate Event Organizer
large-scale-event-ops.imageAlt: Confetti falls over a crowd at a live event, illustrating the scale and timing pressure of large public programs.
large-scale-event-ops.caption: Live programs depend on transitions that hold under pressure. Photograph used as illustration.
large-scale-event-ops.lead: Live programs with large audiences depend on precise transitions, shared timing, and clean backstage coordination. Small breakdowns become visible immediately — there is no quiet draft.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: A transition that is even slightly unclear becomes a visible failure the moment the room is watching. The challenge in large public events is not creating dramatic moments — it is making sure pacing and execution stay calm under pressure that the audience can feel.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: My role sat close to the line between planning and execution: translating the show flow into something technical teams and on-stage participants could actually run without hesitation, supporting transition planning, and keeping pacing tight enough that technical teams, speakers, performers, and audiences stayed in sync.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: Events ran with less transition downtime, clearer stage flow, and more dependable control during moments where timing had to hold under pressure — including Youth Mass 2025, which served as a clear proof point for live communication in front of 500+ participants.

large-scale-event-ops.pull: When pacing holds, the event feels intentional. When it breaks, everyone notices.
evidence: Coordinated technical execution for events with 1,000+ attendees.
MC-led Youth Mass 2025 for 500+ participants while maintaining pacing and clarity on stage.
Reduced visible transition friction through more structured stage workflows.

impact.label: Audience scale
impact.note: Large live-event environments with visible execution pressure.

impact.label: Led as MC
impact.note: Youth Mass 2025 as a proof point for live communication.

vertical-rescue-ops.documentTitle: Vertical Rescue Ops · The Operational Record
vertical-rescue-ops.metaDescription: Equipment readiness, technical training, and operational discipline over 4+ active years at Vertical Rescue Indonesia.
vertical-rescue-ops.title: The quieter part of high-risk work is the part nobody films.
vertical-rescue-ops.deck: Four-plus years of equipment care and training support at Vertical Rescue Indonesia — readiness as a discipline, not a posture.
vertical-rescue-ops.lead: Readiness work is quieter than live delivery, but the standard is higher: equipment, people, and process all have to be dependable before the field ever becomes demanding.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: Technical rescue environments depend on disciplined preparation. Equipment checks, training cadence, and role clarity cannot be improvised once conditions become serious. The work is not producing dramatic moments. It is making sure the fundamentals are correct long before those moments arrive.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: Equipment care, training support, and technical reliability — keeping equipment in inspectable condition, supporting technical climbing as a lead climber and belayer, and helping uphold the training discipline needed for safe and repeatable readiness work.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: Steadier operational readiness, more structured preparation, and stronger support for the people entering technical rescue training environments. The standard, simply, was higher than what live work alone would force.

vertical-rescue-ops.pull: In technical environments, confidence comes from preparation — not improvisation.
evidence: Maintained equipment through structured inspection and readiness routines.
Supported technical training sessions as a lead climber and belayer.
Contributed to a culture where safety and preparation remained visible parts of the work.

impact.label: Years active
impact.note: Sustained involvement in readiness and training work.

impact.label: Equipment discipline
impact.note: Inspection and maintenance as part of the standard.

impact.label: Training support
impact.note: Hands-on contribution in climbing and belay environments.
